synopsis: TCAS warns airline pilots of possible mid-air collisions and advises climbing or descending; it has flown on airliners for decades [f15744, f15745]. ACAS X is its replacement or successor, validated largely through simulation using statistical encounter models of near-collisions [f1428, f15744]. Both systems leave the pilot responsible for flying the maneuver, so their relevance to heavy-machine collision mitigation is as precedents for warning logic rather than automatic braking [f15748]. March 2022 RTCA SC-147 minutes recorded European results suggesting ACAS Xa induced more near mid-air collisions than TCAS, while MIT Lincoln Laboratory did not see the same disparity [f1436, f15754]. This disagreement raises questions about encounter or scenario model representativeness, with sensor noise still unassessed, and warns against relying on a single simulation toolchain [f1968, f1969].
